extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent prosecutors and patent applicants (patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a claimed invention satisfies the statutory utility requirement (35 U.S.C. §101) and related procedural actions (including interplay with 35 U.S.C. §112) during patent examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-world context of use / substantial utility (examples and non-examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed assay or product that measures the presence of a material that has a stated correlation to a predisposition to a disease defines a 'real world' context of use and can establish a substantial utility. Conversely, certain situations do not define 'substantial utilities' and require further research or reasonable confirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-examples that do NOT define substantial utility (require further research): (A) basic research studying properties or mechanisms of the claimed product; (B) a method of treating an unspecified disease or condition; (C) a method of assaying for or identifying a material that itself has no specific/substantial utility; (D) a method of making a material that itself has no specific, substantial, and credible utility; (E) a claim to an intermediate product for use in making a final product that has no specific, substantial and credible utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Immediate benefit to the public" does not require current availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must not interpret phrases like 'immediate benefit to the public' to mean the product or service must already be publicly available to satisfy the utility requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept any reasonable use identified by the applicant that can be viewed as providing a public benefit as sufficient to define a 'substantial' utility (see Brenner v. Manson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Research tools labeling not determinative for utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Labels such as 'research tool,' 'intermediate,' or 'for research purposes' do not determine whether an invention has specific and substantial utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between inventions that actually have a specifically identified substantial utility and inventions whose asserted utility requires further research to identify or reasonably confirm; many research tools (e.g., chromatography instruments, screening assays) have clear specific utilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholly inoperative inventions / 'incredible' utility standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention that is 'inoperative' (does not operate to produce the claimed results) is not useful, but to violate §101 the claimed device must be totally incapable of achieving a useful result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small degree or partial success is sufficient; rejections on inoperability are rare and fact-specific. Do not label asserted utility 'incredible' or 'speculative' unless it is clear the invention cannot and does not work as claimed. Examples of rejected 'inoperative' claims are fact-specific (e.g., perpetual motion, cold fusion, uncharacterized cures for many cancers) and should not be applied as per se rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic/pharmacological utility requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions asserting therapeutic or pharmacological utility are subject to the same utility legal standards as other technologies; identification of pharmacological activity can satisfy practical utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of pharmacological activity provides an immediate public benefit (Nelson v. Bowler). Evidence such as in vitro testing can, under appropriate circumstances, establish practical utility and marshal further development. FDA approval or clinical-phase testing (e.g., Phase II) is not required to satisfy patent-law utility; applicants need not prove safety/effectiveness for market approval under §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: A deficiency under the utility prong of §101 also creates a deficiency under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112, first paragraph); 112 presupposes compliance with 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejection under §101 for lack of utility should be accompanied by a separate rejection under §112(a) that incorporates by reference the factual basis/conclusions of the §101 rejection and explains that, because the invention lacks utility, a person skilled in the art would not be able to use it. Do not impose a §112(a) rejection on lack-of-utility grounds unless an appropriate §101 basis exists. Note that §112(a) also addresses other issues (enablement, written description, best mode) and those rejections should be separate from utility-based rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-level focus: evaluate each claim on its own merits
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention (each claim) is the focus of the utility assessment; each claim must be evaluated individually for compliance with statutory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally, a dependent claim has utility if its independent claim is in the same statutory class and defines an invention having utility. If a genus claim is supported by some species that have utility, treat the genus as sufficient unless it can be established that other species clearly lack utility; in such cases encourage narrowing amendments to exclude non-utility species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single credible assertion of utility suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant need only make one credible assertion of specific utility for the claimed invention to satisfy §101 and §112(a); additional utility statements, even if not credible, do not negate utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements in the specification or prosecution history are not, standing alone, a basis for rejection. If a properly claimed invention meets at least one stated objective, utility under §101 is shown (citing Raytheon v. Roper and other cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asserted utility must be specific and substantial
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of specific and substantial utility should fully and clearly explain why the applicant believes the invention is useful and enable a person of ordinary skill to understand that belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague or generalized assertions (e.g., 'biological activity', 'biological properties', 'plastic-like') without explanation of why that activity makes the invention useful are insufficient under §101. A disclosure that identifies a particular biological activity and explains how it can be used therapeutically does assert specific and substantial utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-established utility can substitute for an explicit assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: If no explicit statement of utility exists in the specification, the invention may nonetheless have a 'well-established utility' that negates the need for an asserted utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements for well-established utility: (i) a person of ordinary skill would immediately appreciate why the invention is useful based on its characteristics, and (ii) the utility is specific, substantial, and credible. If well-established utility exists, do not impose §101/§112 rejections for lack of utility (example: cloning of a well-known protein such as insulin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedural steps when no or questionable asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification lacks a statement asserting specific and substantial utility and no well-established utility exists, the examiner should reject under §101 and §112(a) and require the applicant to explain why the invention is useful and indicate where support for the asserted utility exists in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rejection should clearly indicate that failure to identify a specific and substantial utility is the basis and should direct the applicant to respond by pointing to support in the specification (see MPEP §2701). If the applicant later supplies an assertion of utility, evaluate that assertion according to credibility/evidentiary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility evaluation: presumption of utility and evidentiary standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant's asserted utility creates a presumption of utility that must be rebutted before imposing a lack-of-utility rejection; Office personnel must start by asking whether there is reason to question the truth of the applicant's assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the 'Langer' formulation: a specification disclosure that teaches how to make and use the invention in scope-corresponding terms is presumed to be enabling and truthful unless there is reason to doubt. To overcome the presumption, the examiner must establish by a preponderance of the evidence that one of ordinary skill would question the truth of the asserted utility — i.e., present facts and reasoning showing it is more likely than not that the assertion is false. Do not begin by assuming the assertion false; present countervailing facts and reasoning if disputing the applicant's evidence.
